title: Endoscopy: Do the Right Procedure for the Right Question, Then Own the Result
bottomLine: Endoscopy is valuable when it answers a defined diagnostic, therapeutic or surveillance question. Choose upper endoscopy, colonoscopy or another endoscopic test from the syndrome and alarm features, manage peri-procedural medication/sedation risk, and close the loop on pathology, treatment and surveillance rather than treating procedure completion as the endpoint.
recognize: Appropriate indications include GI bleeding, progressive/alarm dysphagia, selected persistent upper-GI symptoms with alarm or failed appropriate initial management, suspected IBD/celiac or other mucosal disease, colorectal diagnostic/surveillance indications and therapeutic procedures.
Postprocedure pathology can change diagnosis, treatment and surveillance even when the endoscopic appearance seemed reassuring.
differentiate: Uncomplicated dyspepsia in a younger low-risk patient does not automatically require immediate endoscopy; alarm/risk features and response to initial management matter.
Routine screening, diagnostic evaluation of symptoms and post-polypectomy/cancer surveillance are different pathways with different timing.
assessment: Clarify the clinical question, urgency, bleeding/anemia/weight loss/dysphagia or other alarms, prior procedures/pathology, anticoagulants/antiplatelets, cardiopulmonary comorbidity, pregnancy, sedation risk and ability to complete preparation/follow-up.
workup: Order endoscopy only when the expected result can change management and select the correct procedure for the suspected anatomic source.
Review pathology and procedure quality/completeness before deciding that a negative or benign-appearing examination ends the workup.
management: Use the current CAG/specialty and local endoscopy pathway for preparation, sedation, biopsies/interventions and periendoscopic antithrombotic management.
After the procedure, document findings, interventions, complications, treatment changes, pending pathology and the exact follow-up owner/interval.
Urgent/emergent endoscopy is required for selected active GI bleeding, obstruction/food bolus and other time-sensitive syndromes rather than routine outpatient scheduling.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant/antiplatelet interruption depends on the agent, thrombotic risk and procedure/intervention bleeding risk; do not apply one universal hold interval.
Sedation risk and postprocedure driving/activity restrictions require the local procedural protocol.
redFlags: Hemodynamic instability or ongoing major GI bleeding
Complete food-bolus obstruction or inability to handle secretions
Postprocedure severe pain, fever, bleeding, dyspnea or peritonitis
Cancer/high-grade dysplasia pathology without closed-loop referral
counselling: Explain why the procedure is being done, what preparation is required, what complications warrant urgent care, and that pathology/follow-up may arrive after the procedure day.
followUp: Track pathology, treatment recommendations and recall/surveillance to completion; ensure the patient and responsible clinician receive the result and plan.
examTrap: Ordering endoscopy because a test exists rather than because it answers a management question—or assuming care is complete when the scope is finished but pathology is still pending.
oneLinePearl: Good endoscopy care has three parts: appropriate indication, safe procedure, closed-loop result and follow-up.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology Guideline Library
Canadian Association of Gastroenterology endoscopy safety and quality indicators

title: Nutritional Assessment: Find the Cause of Malnutrition Before Prescribing Supplements
bottomLine: Nutrition assessment is more than BMI or albumin. Identify recent intake and weight trajectory, muscle/function loss, GI losses or malabsorption, swallowing/dental barriers, inflammatory disease, medications, food insecurity and micronutrient risk; then match oral, enteral, parenteral or targeted supplementation to the cause and severity.
recognize: Unintentional weight loss, reduced intake, loss of muscle/function, recurrent dehydration, micronutrient deficiency and inability to meet needs are clinically important even when BMI is not low.
Albumin is affected by inflammation and illness and should not be used alone to diagnose protein-calorie malnutrition.
differentiate: Poor intake, malabsorption, increased metabolic need and nutrient loss require different interventions.
Intentional weight change, fluid-related weight change and true tissue loss must be distinguished.
A restrictive diet prescribed for a symptom can itself create nutrient deficiency if not clinically justified and monitored.
assessment: Document usual/current intake, recent percentage/tempo of weight change, GI symptoms, stool/ostomy losses, swallowing/chewing, medications/supplements, alcohol/substance use, pregnancy, functional status and food/access barriers.
Examine hydration, muscle/fat loss, edema, oral health and disease-specific deficiency signs where relevant.
workup: Use CBC, electrolytes/renal function and cause-directed iron, B12, folate, vitamin D or other micronutrient testing when the history/disease makes deficiency plausible; avoid indiscriminate supplement panels.
Investigate celiac disease, pancreatic insufficiency, IBD, malignancy or other causes when malabsorption/weight loss has a compatible syndrome.
management: Use food-first/oral nutrition support when the GI tract works and needs can be met safely; involve a registered dietitian for significant malnutrition, complex disease or therapeutic diets.

Use enteral nutrition when oral intake is inadequate but the gut is usable; parenteral nutrition is reserved for intestinal failure or other situations where enteral intake/absorption cannot meet needs and requires specialist monitoring.
Correct identified micronutrient deficits with cause- and dose-appropriate therapy rather than indefinite broad supplementation.
medicationSafety: Refeeding syndrome risk requires cautious nutrition advancement and electrolyte/thiamine monitoring in severely malnourished high-risk patients.
Iron, calcium, magnesium and other supplements can interact with medications and cause toxicity when used unnecessarily; renal/hepatic disease changes some replacement plans.
redFlags: Severe or rapid unintentional weight loss
Severe electrolyte disturbance or vitamin deficiency with neurologic/cardiac effects
counselling: Use non-stigmatizing language and include food cost, culture, disability and access in the plan rather than reducing nutrition care to willpower.
Explain why a targeted supplement is being used and when it will be reassessed.
followUp: Track weight trajectory, intake, function, hydration, relevant labs and whether the underlying cause is being treated; stop or adjust supplementation when the indication changes.
examTrap: Diagnosing malnutrition from low albumin alone—or prescribing a broad vitamin panel and supplements without identifying why the patient is losing weight or failing to absorb nutrients.
oneLinePearl: Nutrition treatment follows mechanism: intake, absorption, loss and metabolic need are different problems.
sourceBasis: Canadian gastroenterology and clinical-nutrition practice principles
Canada's Food Guide for general dietary pattern where applicable

title: Short Bowel Syndrome: Replace Fluid and Nutrients While the Intestine Adapts
bottomLine: Short bowel syndrome causes intestinal failure when remaining bowel cannot maintain hydration, electrolytes and nutrition without specialized support. Management depends on the anatomy left behind, colon continuity, ostomy output and adaptation phase; protect hydration and renal function, maximize safe enteral/oral absorption, replace deficiencies and use parenteral support only to the degree still required.
recognize: High-output diarrhea/ostomy, dehydration, electrolyte or magnesium disturbance, weight loss and micronutrient deficiency are common.
Loss of terminal ileum can impair bile-salt and vitamin B12 absorption; loss of colon or extensive small bowel changes fluid/energy salvage and oxalate/stone risk.
Needs can improve during intestinal adaptation, so long-term support should be reassessed rather than assumed permanent at the initial level.
differentiate: SBS is not simply chronic diarrhea: the remaining anatomy predicts fluid, nutrient and medication absorption problems.
High ostomy output can reflect infection, obstruction, medication effect or active bowel disease in addition to reduced absorptive length.
Dehydration can occur despite drinking large volumes of hypotonic fluid because sodium/water absorption physiology is altered in some high-output patients.
assessment: Document original surgery/cause, bowel length/anatomy when known, colon and ileocecal-valve continuity, ostomy/stool output, oral/enteral/parenteral intake, urine output, weight, kidney stones, medications and prior micronutrient deficiencies.
Assess orthostasis, dehydration, edema, muscle loss and central-line complications where parenteral nutrition is used.
workup: Trend electrolytes, magnesium, renal function, hydration and disease/anatomy-specific micronutrients; monitor liver/bone/metabolic complications when long-term parenteral support is required.
Investigate abrupt increases in output for infection, obstruction, active inflammatory disease or medication causes rather than assuming expected SBS physiology.
management: Use a specialized intestinal-failure/gastroenterology dietitian team to individualize meal pattern, oral rehydration composition, enteral feeding and parenteral fluid/nutrition based on anatomy and output.
Use antimotility, acid-suppression or other absorption-focused therapies selectively according to the phase/anatomy and specialist plan; avoid one universal drug regimen.
Protect central-line safety and taper parenteral support only when hydration, weight and biochemical status remain adequate.
medicationSafety: Drug absorption can be unpredictable after major bowel resection; modified-release or poorly absorbed formulations may fail and require pharmacist/specialist review.
Long-term parenteral nutrition carries catheter infection/thrombosis and hepatobiliary/metabolic risks that require structured monitoring.
Do not recommend unrestricted plain water alone for a high-output patient whose sodium losses require a specific oral rehydration strategy.
redFlags: Severe dehydration or acute kidney injury
Severe malnutrition or inability to maintain weight/hydration
counselling: Teach output and hydration/urine warning signs, the individualized oral-rehydration and diet plan, medication-absorption issues and central-line infection symptoms if applicable.
Acknowledge the cost and burden of specialized foods, supplies and nutrition support and connect patients with available provincial assistance/resources.
followUp: Use coordinated intestinal-failure, dietitian and pharmacy follow-up to reassess adaptation, parenteral needs, renal/liver/bone health and micronutrients.
After hospitalization or surgery, ensure exact bowel anatomy and current fluid/nutrition prescriptions are communicated at transitions of care.
examTrap: Telling a high-output SBS patient simply to drink more plain water and take a multivitamin while ignoring sodium losses, altered absorption, anatomy and the need for intestinal-failure nutrition support.
oneLinePearl: Short bowel care is anatomy-driven fluid and nutrition physiology, not generic diarrhea treatment.
sourceBasis: International short-bowel syndrome nutrition guidance used where no current Canadian national SBS CPG is available
